title: The answer
heading: A garment, and a set of rules
intro: Both. Becke defines kimono by <q>the garment's shape and practice of fitting it to the body</q> {4:p.10}.
rules: A fold of cloth beneath the obi {4:p.71}
No motifs of a season that has passed {6:p.27}
The flower a month before it blooms {4:p.62}
Black crested haori: the most formal {37:P-386}
Edo: silk above, cotton and hemp below {39:p.438}

line.text: Both: the cloth, and the way it is worn.

closing: Real photographs and hand-built 3D; nothing generated. Narration: synthetic voice (Venice AI).

cues.show: Walk back down the hall now. Past the prints, past the robes, to the flat robe on its rack.
Becke's thesis follows the furisode at the coming-of-age day. But her definition is a general one. It covers the whole family you have just passed.
The shape is the plain part. Unworn, a kimono is completely flat. No darts, no tucks, nothing to hold a body's form.
The practice is the rest. A kimono maker, Yamaguchi Genbei, put a figure on it: seventy percent of what makes a kimono a kimono is how it is worn. That is a maker's view, not a measurement.
cues.say: The practice is the rest. A kimono maker, Yah-mah-goo-chee Ghen-bay, put a figure on it: seventy percent of what makes a kimono a kimono is how it is worn. That is a maker's view, not a measurement.

cues.show: And the practice has a history. Laws on cloth under the shoguns. After the war, one book with three hundred and ninety rules.
So the answer is both. A garment, and a set of rules. Whichever you chose at the entrance, you were holding half of it.
Becke adds one more thing. Rules can be bent, she writes, and clothes altered.
The robe stays on its rack, flat, until someone puts it on. Thank you for walking with us.

claims.text: Becke defines kimono as a category of dress based on the garment's shape and the practice of fitting it.
claims.quote: a general category of dress which is based on the garment's shape and practice of fitting it to the body
claims.scope: Becke; general definition, although her thesis is about the furisode at the coming-of-age day

claims.text: Unworn, a kimono has a completely flat surface.
claims.quote: In its unworn form, a kimono has a completely flat surface.

claims.text: No tucks or darts give the kimono a three-dimensional shape.
claims.quote: no tucks or darts are added to the fabric which would provide the garment with a three-dimensional shape

claims.text: Seventy percent of what makes a kimono a kimono is how it is worn.
claims.quote: 'Seventy percent of what makes a kimono a kimono is how it is worn'
claims.scope: reported: Yamaguchi Genbei, head of the kimono house Kondaya Genbei, quoted by Becke; a maker's view, not an academic finding

claims.text: The Tokugawa government issued sumptuary laws on what each class could wear.
claims.quote: issuing sumptuary laws on the type of clothes members of each class were allowed to wear

claims.text: A 1972 book contains 390 rules on buying, choosing and wearing kimono.
claims.quote: The book contains a total of 390 rules in regards to buying, choosing, and wearing kimono.
claims.scope: Shiotsuki, Kimono no Hon, 1972, as described by Becke

claims.text: Rules can be bent and clothes modified.
claims.quote: Rules can be bended and pieces of clothing can be modified, however

claims.text: The kimono is draped from the left side over to the right.
claims.quote: without exception always draped from the left side over to the right

claims.text: Dressing runs from the nagajuban to the obi knot.
claims.quote: from putting on the nagajuban (under-kimono) to the final tying of the obi knot
claims.scope: furisode; magazine columns; only these two steps are ordered

claims.text: The ohashori is a fold of fabric beneath the obi.
claims.quote: the creation of an ohashori, the fold of fabric beneath the obi

claims.text: The lined kimono is appropriate from October until May.
claims.quote: with awase (袷 lined kimono), one can enjoy an outfit that would be appropriate from October until May

claims.text: The unlined kimono is for the warm months.
claims.quote: With hitoe (単衣 unlined kimono) it is the lightness of the fabric that is appreciated, especially during the warm months
claims.scope: Druet 2024; the sentence ends 'that spread from June to September'

claims.text: Wearing the motifs of a past season is a faux pas.
claims.quote: dressing in hues or motifs that are of the passed / past season would be considered a major “fashion faux-pas”
claims.scope: Druet 2024; general. Elsewhere (p.22) she calls seasonal dress 'not mandatory but strongly encouraged'

claims.text: One guide says to wear a flower pattern about a month before the flower blooms.
claims.quote: start wearing a specific flower pattern about one month ahead of the actual blossoming of the drawn flower
claims.scope: reported: Becke quoting Shimada 2017, a guide; advice, not observed practice

claims.text: Repeated all-over komon patterns are considered less formal.
claims.quote: pervasive and repetitive patterns called komon are generally considered less formal
claims.scope: reported: Dalby, Ōkubo, kimono association, via Becke

claims.text: The furisode is mainly for unmarried women.
claims.quote: mainly reserved for unmarried women to wear at formal occasions

claims.text: In mid-Edo the black crested haori became the most formal.
claims.quote: 江戸中期には黒紋付（羽二重・縮緬など）が最も正式なものとなる。 (Tr. "in mid-Edo the black crested [haori] (habutae, crepe) became the most formal")
claims.scope: Yokogawa 2008, invited essay, not refereed; men's haori

claims.text: In the early shogunate rank was shown by material: silk above, then pongee, cotton and hemp.
claims.quote: 幕政初期には上位の者に絹,続いて紬,木綿,布と衣服材料でもって身分差を示そうとした (Tr. "in the early shogunate they tried to show rank by material: silk for those above, then tsumugi, cotton and hemp cloth")
claims.scope: Nishimura 1980, refereed; Edo period, hence 'Edo:' on the rule

dropped: A single date when 'the rules' were fixed: the sources point to Meiji for the shape (4 p.72) and to the post-war decades for standardised dressing (4 p.11), so no one date is given.
Rules on crests by number and on collar depth by age or profession: no source read gives a general rule.
Labels on the back of the robe: left out on purpose; the rules carry the room.
